task.goal: Teach 20 adult learners to spot when a recipe scaling calculation changes cooking time assumptions, not just ingredient quantities.
hard_constraints: One 40-minute classroom session with printed recipes and no kitchen or devices.
Avoid food allergy disclosures or real food preparation.
Assess a new scaling scenario individually, requiring a safe test or observation rather than an invented fixed cooking-time formula.
task.available_resources: Fictional small and large batch recipe cards.
task.expected_result: A clear lesson with transfer assessment and uncertainty handling.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Contrast pairs: same quantity, different cooking conditions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare recipe pairs that scale ingredients identically but change different physical conditions. This separates quantity arithmetic from assumptions about heating. Use fictional baked-dish cards: one large batch is divided among matching shallow pans; another is placed in one deeper vessel. Neither card supplies a new cooking time. What changes the outcome is recognizing that depth, vessel, oven loading, and starting temperature can matter independently of ingredient multipliers.

Run one 40-minute session for 20 adults: 5 minutes introducing quantity versus cooking assumptions; 10 minutes comparing cards in ten pairs; 8 minutes discussing which original assumptions remain plausible; 5 minutes practicing a conditional instruction; 10 minutes completing an individual transfer task; 2 minutes collecting responses. The conditional instruction follows: ‘We cannot infer the time from the ingredient multiplier. Check ___, using ___; if ___, then ___.’

Resources are printed fictional recipe cards, including written response spaces and an instructor key. Cards must state vessel dimensions, batch placement, starting conditions, and a recipe-specific safe endpoint supplied for the exercise. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

The new individual scenario changes both batch size and vessel depth. Learners identify the broken assumption, explain why an exact time is uncertain, and propose a safe observation: for example, an adult cook checks the coldest central area with an appropriate thermometer against the supplied endpoint and continues cooking and rechecks if necessary. Color alone is insufficient where the card specifies a temperature endpoint. Limits: classroom answers demonstrate planning, not practical cooking competence; matching depth also does not guarantee identical timing.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give ten randomly selected learners a contrasting pair and ten an equally long ingredient-scaling example before a short individual probe; then teach everyone the full lesson. Compare recognition of changed heating assumptions and selection of a safe check. The mechanism is weakened if contrast-pair learners merely repeat ‘time varies’ without naming the changed condition or an adequate observation. Use the final unseen scenario to inspect individual transfer; treat this small comparison as diagnostic, not proof of effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Assumption audit: turn a recipe into conditional instructions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners reconstruct the conditions under which an original cooking instruction could be reasonable, then audit those conditions after scaling. Instead of guessing a new duration, they learn to treat the original time as conditional information. The key move is asking what must remain true before reusing an instruction.

Use printed fictional small- and large-batch recipe cards with response areas. Include ingredient amounts, portion thickness, vessel dimensions, starting temperature, equipment loading, and a supplied safe endpoint. Some large-batch details should deliberately be unspecified. Learners classify cooking-related claims as ‘supported,’ ‘changed,’ or ‘unknown,’ and attach a question or observation to each important unknown. This requires sufficient reading fluency and clearly written cards; the instructor can read directions aloud without adding equipment.

The 40 minutes comprise a 5-minute worked audit, 9 minutes auditing in five groups of four, 8 minutes exchanging and challenging audits, 6 minutes revising instructions, 10 minutes of individual transfer, and 2 minutes collecting work. No food is handled and no personal dietary information is requested.

The individual transfer card describes a scaled casserole but omits the final depth. Each learner must explain why the ingredient multiplier does not establish cooking time, identify the missing depth information, and write a safe plan conditional on it. An acceptable plan requests vessel or depth information and still checks the supplied safe endpoint at an appropriate location before serving; it does not invent a time multiplier. What changes the outcome is converting uncertainty into a specific information request and verification action. A limit is that learners may produce elaborate audits without prioritizing consequential assumptions, so require them to identify the single most important unknown and justify it.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before teaching, give everyone a two-minute fictional scaling prompt asking what they would do next. Compare it with the final individual audit using three criteria: identifies a consequential assumption, acknowledges timing uncertainty, and proposes an adequate safe check. The simple comparator is ordinary ingredient-multiplier reasoning visible in the initial response. The mechanism is challenged if learners label details ‘unknown’ but cannot explain how obtaining the information would change their plan. Different prompts and the small class limit causal conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Decision rehearsal: revise a plan when observations arrive
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners practice updating a cooking decision from evidence rather than committing to a calculated finishing time. Printed observation branches make the consequences of a time-only rule visible without cooking anything. The branches are fictional teaching examples, not measured results or universal timing guidance.

Prepare recipe-card sets containing an original recipe, a scaled version, a supplied safe endpoint, and folded observation panels. For a fictional deep baked dish, panels might report that the surface appears finished while the center remains below the supplied endpoint, or that different central locations give inconsistent readings. Learners choose their next action before opening the corresponding panel: serve, continue cooking and recheck, or gather a better observation. The card explains why elapsed time and appearance alone cannot settle the decision.

For 20 adults, use ten pairs. Spend 5 minutes establishing the distinction between scaled quantities and uncertain cooking duration; 12 minutes working through two branches; 8 minutes discussing which evidence justified each decision; 5 minutes writing a reusable checking plan; 8 minutes on an individual unseen scenario; and 2 minutes collecting answers. All activity uses printed fictional recipes; there is no food preparation, device use, or allergy discussion.

The transfer scenario changes the geometry—for example, a doubled mixture becomes fewer, thicker individual portions. Each learner must name the changed assumption and propose a safe future check against the supplied endpoint, including what to do if it is unmet. They may describe thermometer use by a future cook; no device is used in class. What changes the outcome is rehearsing a conditional action loop: inspect, interpret, continue or stop, and recheck. Prerequisites are explicit endpoint instructions and branches that allow meaningful choices. Limits: scripted observations cannot establish real cooking duration, and success may reflect following branches unless the unseen assessment removes those prompts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: On the individual transfer card, first ask learners to write their next action without answer choices; only afterward provide a short list of possible observations. Compare the unprompted plan with their original pre-branch decision, the simple comparator. Look for replacement of fixed-time confidence with a justified safe checking loop. The mechanism is weakened if learners choose correct actions only when branches supply them, or transfer ‘keep cooking’ mechanically even when reliable endpoint evidence supports stopping. Inspect all 20 responses; no actual cooking outcome is claimed.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Error inoculation: correct a convincing but invalid worked solution
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners explain and repair a persuasive scaling error. A fictional worked solution correctly triples ingredient quantities, then incorrectly concludes that cooking time must also triple. Learners must pinpoint where valid arithmetic stops supporting the conclusion. Generating a rebuttal could help them resist the appeal of a tidy calculation when a later recipe changes heating conditions.

Use printed fictional recipe cards with ingredient amounts, vessel dimensions, mixture depth, starting conditions, and a recipe-specific safe endpoint. Print the flawed solution and response spaces on the cards. Assume learners can follow simple multiplication; the instructor can read the text aloud. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are needed.

For 20 adults, spend 4 minutes on an individual opening question; 6 minutes explaining the difference between a numerical mistake and an unsupported inference; 10 minutes having ten pairs annotate the flawed solution; 8 minutes having pairs write and exchange corrections; 10 minutes on individual transfer; and 2 minutes collecting responses. Require corrections to preserve the valid ingredient arithmetic, reject the unsupported time calculation, explain how changed depth affects confidence in timing, and specify evidence needed before serving. The instructor explicitly resolves the error before assessment so the false rule is not left unchallenged.

The unseen individual assessment uses a smaller batch formed into thicker portions. Without a worked answer, each learner explains why reduced quantity does not establish a shorter cooking time and describes a future cook checking the supplied endpoint at the specified central locations, continuing cooking and rechecking if it is unmet. No exact finishing time is requested.

What changes the outcome is practicing a precise rebuttal to an attractive invalid inference. Limits: learners might memorize ‘never multiply time’ without understanding heating conditions; written success also cannot establish practical cooking competence.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the opening question as a simple comparator: present an ingredient multiplier and ask whether it establishes a cooking-time multiplier, with a reason. Inspect all 20 final responses for recognition of changed thickness, explicit timing uncertainty, and an adequate endpoint-checking plan. The mechanism is challenged if learners reject multiplication but replace it with another unsupported fixed rule, or cannot explain why thickness matters. Different opening and final scenarios prevent a clean causal estimate; this is a small classroom check of transfer, not evidence of proven effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Trace the heat path: build a spatial explanation before choosing a check
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners use printed recipe cross-sections to explain how heat reaches the least-heated part of a dish. They trace inward from heated surfaces and mark locations that may lag behind. This builds a causal model connecting scaling to geometry: multiplying ingredients can change the distance heat must travel, while ingredient arithmetic alone cannot establish a finishing time. The drawing supports qualitative reasoning, not a heat-transfer calculation.

For 20 adults, prepare ten shared practice sets and 20 individual assessment cards. Fictional recipe cards include ingredient quantities, vessel cross-sections, portion dimensions, starting conditions, and explicit recipe-specific safe endpoint instructions. Learners need pens and basic diagram-reading ability; the instructor can explain diagrams aloud. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

Use 6 minutes to demonstrate tracing heat through a simple cross-section, 10 minutes for ten pairs to annotate a scaled recipe, 8 minutes for pairs to explain their marked locations, 6 minutes to connect those locations to safe checking plans, and 10 minutes for individual transfer. Explain that actual heating also depends on composition, equipment, and loading; a diagram cannot identify an exact coldest point or predict duration.

The unseen assessment scales a fictional baked mixture into thicker portions despite reducing total quantity. Each learner marks potentially slow-heating regions, explains which original cooking assumption has changed, and describes a future cook using an appropriate thermometer at the locations specified by the card. The plan must compare readings with the supplied safe endpoint and continue cooking and recheck if it is unmet. Exact cooking time remains uncertain. What changes the outcome is a spatial explanation learners can reconstruct when ingredient multipliers are misleading. The main limitation is that simplified drawings may encourage overconfidence about real heat flow.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before instruction, collect a brief individual response to a comparable scaling scenario described in words. Compare all 20 final responses with this baseline for an explained geometry change and a safe endpoint-checking plan. As a falsifying check, give the final scenario without a cross-section: if learners cannot reconstruct the relevant thickness change, or merely state that the center always determines safety without following the supplied checking instructions, the proposed spatial mechanism has weak support. This small classroom comparison checks transfer, not practical cooking competence or causal effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Build a paper model of the heating problem
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners construct a simple spatial model showing why scaling ingredients does not determine heating time. Making the distance from a heated surface to the interior visible gives them a causal explanation they can apply beyond a memorized warning that ‘time varies.’ This differs from auditing recipe conditions: learners first build an explanation of why a changed condition matters.

Use fictional recipe cards with printed cross-sections of a shallow baked dish and blank grids for drawing scaled arrangements. In ten pairs, learners represent a doubled quantity in two possible arrangements, mark the surfaces receiving heat, and trace a possible route toward the center. They then explain why doubling quantity alone cannot tell them how long the center takes to reach the supplied safe endpoint. The instructor explicitly states that the drawing is qualitative: heat enters through several surfaces, and distance is not a cooking-time formula.

Allocate 6 minutes to an instructor model, 10 to paired drawings, 8 to explanations and corrections, 6 to writing checking instructions, and 10 to individual transfer. Resources are printed cards, pencils, and an instructor key. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

The unseen individual scenario scales a recipe into thicker portions. Each learner identifies the changed heating distance, rejects an exact time inferred from quantity, and describes a future cook checking the supplied recipe-specific safe endpoint at the specified interior locations, continuing and rechecking if necessary.

Prerequisites are readable diagrams and instructor guidance that prevents treating the picture as a quantitative model. The mechanism could help by connecting a visible geometric change to an otherwise invisible heating process. Its limits include differences in equipment, material, and starting temperature; the classroom task establishes explanatory planning, not practical competence.
EXPAND.experiment: Before instruction, give ten learners the drawing task and ten an equally long ingredient-calculation exercise, followed by the same brief individual prompt. Then provide the full model lesson to everyone. Inspect whether drawings produce more explanations connecting changed thickness to uncertain interior heating and an adequate endpoint check. A small falsifying result would be equally frequent fixed-time rules in both groups, or drawing learners claiming that doubled distance means doubled time. Use the final unseen scenario to check all 20 learners individually. This small classroom comparison is diagnostic, not evidence of reliable effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Repair a convincing but unsafe worked solution
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair an attractive reasoning error: correct ingredient arithmetic followed by an unsupported cooking-time calculation. Explicitly separating a valid step from an invalid inference may help adults resist the apparent authority of a neatly worked numerical answer. The central activity is explaining why a plausible solution fails, rather than comparing recipes or rehearsing observation branches.

Prepare printed fictional recipe cards and an accompanying fictional learner solution. For example, the solution correctly triples each ingredient, then triples the cooking time despite placing the mixture in a deeper vessel. Label this as a deliberately flawed teaching example. Supply the original cooking conditions and a recipe-specific safe endpoint. Include another solution that retains the original time with unjustified certainty, so learners do not replace ‘multiply time’ with ‘never change time.’

For 20 adults, spend 5 minutes introducing the task, 7 individually annotating the first solution, 8 discussing repairs in ten pairs, 7 reviewing the second error, 3 writing a replacement instruction, and 10 on individual transfer. All work uses printed materials and pencils; there is no cooking, device use, or request for dietary information.

The transfer card presents a new scaled recipe without a worked answer. Each learner must identify a changed cooking assumption, explain why quantity arithmetic cannot establish the finishing time, and specify a safe future observation against the supplied endpoint, including continuing and rechecking if it is unmet. A time estimate alone does not pass.

What changes the outcome is learning to locate the unsupported inference while preserving the correct arithmetic. Prerequisites include accessible calculations and a clear correction immediately after discussion. Limits include possible reinforcement of the misleading example and learners becoming indiscriminately suspicious of all timing guidance; explicitly retain original times as conditional planning information.
EXPAND.experiment: Before the discussion, randomly give half the class the flawed worked solution and half a correct explanation of equal length. Ask both groups to explain the decision on a short new prompt, then teach everyone the complete correction. Compare identification of the unsupported time inference and inclusion of a safe endpoint check. The mechanism is weakened if error diagnosis produces more fixed-time claims, or learners can criticize the supplied answer but cannot generate a safe plan without it. Score the final independent scenario for transfer; do not infer actual cooking safety or durable learning from this single session.

EXPAND.title: Instruction handoff: make a cooking plan survive another reader
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners discover unsupported timing assumptions through communication failure. One learner writes instructions for a future cook; another interprets them literally, without access to the writer’s intentions. The writer must then repair any instruction that permits serving on elapsed time alone. What changes the outcome is feedback about what another person can actually decide from the instructions, rather than agreement that scaling can affect cooking time.

Use ten pairs and printed fictional small- and large-batch recipe cards with response spaces. Each card supplies quantities, vessel arrangement, starting conditions, and a recipe-specific safe endpoint with appropriate checking locations. Include two large-batch arrangements, such as several shallow vessels and one deeper vessel. Cards explicitly state that actual finishing times are unknown. Pencils are the only additional materials.

Allocate 5 minutes to explaining the task, 6 to individual instruction writing, 8 to paired literal interpretation, 7 to revision, 4 to extracting a reusable communication rule, and 10 to individual transfer. During interpretation, the reader marks what authorizes serving, what remains unknown, and whether the instruction explains what to do when the endpoint is unmet. Writers cannot clarify orally until the reader finishes. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

The unseen transfer card changes portion thickness and equipment loading. Individually, learners identify a changed cooking assumption and write a self-contained instruction for a future cook. Passing requires acknowledging uncertain timing, checking the supplied safe endpoint at the specified locations, and continuing cooking and rechecking if necessary. A calculated duration alone cannot pass.

This could work because vague understanding becomes visible as an unusable instruction. It assumes adequate reading fluency and explicit endpoint guidance. Its limits are that polished writing can conceal weak understanding and paper interpretation cannot establish practical cooking competence; accept concise bullets or annotated drawings.
EXPAND.experiment: For a small classroom pilot, give five randomly selected pairs the literal-reader handoff and five pairs equal-time solo revision using the same cards and endpoint guidance. Both groups complete the same individual transfer task. Score anonymous responses for a justified changed assumption, uncertainty about duration, and an actionable endpoint-and-recheck plan. The mechanism is challenged if handoff participants produce no more complete plans, or merely improve wording while retaining time-only serving decisions. With ten learners per condition, treat any difference as preliminary; inspect actual errors before retaining the activity.

REFINE.title: Repair candidate 0: make the contrast isolate depth
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate index: 0. Its contrast-pair mechanism offers strong task fit and classroom feasibility, but its examples change vessel, depth and oven loading together. Learners could notice that cooking conditions differ without identifying which assumption the ingredient multiplier fails to preserve.

Change only the comparison cards: use a fictional casserole whose original batch fills one rectangular pan to 2 cm. Both doubled versions use two identical pans, the same total mixture, starting temperature and stated oven positions. Version A distributes the mixture evenly, reaching 2 cm in each pan; version B distributes it unevenly, reaching 1 cm and 3 cm. Print matching cross-section diagrams. Ask pairs to identify what is held constant, what changes, and whether either version has a guaranteed finishing time. The useful distinction is that A preserves the original depth while B does not; neither establishes a cooking-time formula, and the extra oven load still limits reuse of the original timing.

Retain the 40-minute session for 20 adults: 5 minutes introducing quantities versus cooking assumptions, 10 comparing cards in ten pairs, 8 discussing assumptions, 5 writing conditional checking instructions, 10 completing individual transfer, and 2 collecting responses. The unseen transfer uses a smaller total batch formed into thicker portions. Each learner must identify the changed thickness, explain timing uncertainty, and describe a future cook checking the supplied safe endpoint at the specified central locations, continuing cooking and rechecking if unmet.

Prerequisites: printed cards with response spaces, readable diagrams, and an explicit recipe-specific safe temperature endpoint and checking locations. Thermometer checks are written plans only; no food, devices, preparation or allergy disclosures enter the classroom. Remaining limit: this controlled comparison simplifies actual cooking, and written answers assess planning rather than practical competence.
REFINE.experiment: Smallest falsifying check: on the individual transfer card, include the claim ‘There is less mixture, so it must finish sooner’ and require an unprompted correction plus a safe checking plan. Score separately whether each learner identifies greater thickness, rejects a guaranteed duration, and specifies checking the supplied endpoint with a continue-and-recheck response if unmet. The repair is challenged if learners reject the claim but cannot connect their decision to thickness or provide an adequate check. Inspect all 20 responses; do not treat this classroom check as proof of causal effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Contrast pairs: same quantity, different cooking conditions
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare recipe pairs that scale ingredients identically but change different physical conditions. This separates quantity arithmetic from assumptions about heating. Use fictional baked-dish cards: one large batch is divided among matching shallow pans; another is placed in one deeper vessel. Neither card supplies a new cooking time. What changes the outcome is recognizing that depth, vessel, oven loading, and starting temperature can matter independently of ingredient multipliers.

Run one 40-minute session for 20 adults: 5 minutes introducing quantity versus cooking assumptions; 10 minutes comparing cards in ten pairs; 8 minutes discussing which original assumptions remain plausible; 5 minutes practicing a conditional instruction; 10 minutes completing an individual transfer task; 2 minutes collecting responses. The conditional instruction follows: ‘We cannot infer the time from the ingredient multiplier. Check ___, using ___; if ___, then ___.’

Resources are printed fictional recipe cards, including written response spaces and an instructor key. Cards must state vessel dimensions, batch placement, starting conditions, and a recipe-specific safe endpoint supplied for the exercise. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

The new individual scenario changes both batch size and vessel depth. Learners identify the broken assumption, explain why an exact time is uncertain, and propose a safe observation: for example, an adult cook checks the coldest central area with an appropriate thermometer against the supplied endpoint and continues cooking and rechecks if necessary. Color alone is insufficient where the card specifies a temperature endpoint. Limits: classroom answers demonstrate planning, not practical cooking competence; matching depth also does not guarantee identical timing.
SAVE.experiment: Give ten randomly selected learners a contrasting pair and ten an equally long ingredient-scaling example before a short individual probe; then teach everyone the full lesson. Compare recognition of changed heating assumptions and selection of a safe check. The mechanism is weakened if contrast-pair learners merely repeat ‘time varies’ without naming the changed condition or an adequate observation. Use the final unseen scenario to inspect individual transfer; treat this small comparison as diagnostic, not proof of effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Assumption audit: turn a recipe into conditional instructions
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: learners reconstruct the conditions under which an original cooking instruction could be reasonable, then audit those conditions after scaling. Instead of guessing a new duration, they learn to treat the original time as conditional information. The key move is asking what must remain true before reusing an instruction.

Use printed fictional small- and large-batch recipe cards with response areas. Include ingredient amounts, portion thickness, vessel dimensions, starting temperature, equipment loading, and a supplied safe endpoint. Some large-batch details should deliberately be unspecified. Learners classify cooking-related claims as ‘supported,’ ‘changed,’ or ‘unknown,’ and attach a question or observation to each important unknown. This requires sufficient reading fluency and clearly written cards; the instructor can read directions aloud without adding equipment.

The 40 minutes comprise a 5-minute worked audit, 9 minutes auditing in five groups of four, 8 minutes exchanging and challenging audits, 6 minutes revising instructions, 10 minutes of individual transfer, and 2 minutes collecting work. No food is handled and no personal dietary information is requested.

The individual transfer card describes a scaled casserole but omits the final depth. Each learner must explain why the ingredient multiplier does not establish cooking time, identify the missing depth information, and write a safe plan conditional on it. An acceptable plan requests vessel or depth information and still checks the supplied safe endpoint at an appropriate location before serving; it does not invent a time multiplier. What changes the outcome is converting uncertainty into a specific information request and verification action. A limit is that learners may produce elaborate audits without prioritizing consequential assumptions, so require them to identify the single most important unknown and justify it.
SAVE.experiment: Before teaching, give everyone a two-minute fictional scaling prompt asking what they would do next. Compare it with the final individual audit using three criteria: identifies a consequential assumption, acknowledges timing uncertainty, and proposes an adequate safe check. The simple comparator is ordinary ingredient-multiplier reasoning visible in the initial response. The mechanism is challenged if learners label details ‘unknown’ but cannot explain how obtaining the information would change their plan. Different prompts and the small class limit causal conclusions.

SAVE.title: Decision rehearsal: revise a plan when observations arrive
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: learners practice updating a cooking decision from evidence rather than committing to a calculated finishing time. Printed observation branches make the consequences of a time-only rule visible without cooking anything. The branches are fictional teaching examples, not measured results or universal timing guidance.

Prepare recipe-card sets containing an original recipe, a scaled version, a supplied safe endpoint, and folded observation panels. For a fictional deep baked dish, panels might report that the surface appears finished while the center remains below the supplied endpoint, or that different central locations give inconsistent readings. Learners choose their next action before opening the corresponding panel: serve, continue cooking and recheck, or gather a better observation. The card explains why elapsed time and appearance alone cannot settle the decision.

For 20 adults, use ten pairs. Spend 5 minutes establishing the distinction between scaled quantities and uncertain cooking duration; 12 minutes working through two branches; 8 minutes discussing which evidence justified each decision; 5 minutes writing a reusable checking plan; 8 minutes on an individual unseen scenario; and 2 minutes collecting answers. All activity uses printed fictional recipes; there is no food preparation, device use, or allergy discussion.

The transfer scenario changes the geometry—for example, a doubled mixture becomes fewer, thicker individual portions. Each learner must name the changed assumption and propose a safe future check against the supplied endpoint, including what to do if it is unmet. They may describe thermometer use by a future cook; no device is used in class. What changes the outcome is rehearsing a conditional action loop: inspect, interpret, continue or stop, and recheck. Prerequisites are explicit endpoint instructions and branches that allow meaningful choices. Limits: scripted observations cannot establish real cooking duration, and success may reflect following branches unless the unseen assessment removes those prompts.
SAVE.experiment: On the individual transfer card, first ask learners to write their next action without answer choices; only afterward provide a short list of possible observations. Compare the unprompted plan with their original pre-branch decision, the simple comparator. Look for replacement of fixed-time confidence with a justified safe checking loop. The mechanism is weakened if learners choose correct actions only when branches supply them, or transfer ‘keep cooking’ mechanically even when reliable endpoint evidence supports stopping. Inspect all 20 responses; no actual cooking outcome is claimed.

SAVE.title: Build a paper model of the heating problem
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: learners construct a simple spatial model showing why scaling ingredients does not determine heating time. Making the distance from a heated surface to the interior visible gives them a causal explanation they can apply beyond a memorized warning that ‘time varies.’ This differs from auditing recipe conditions: learners first build an explanation of why a changed condition matters.

Use fictional recipe cards with printed cross-sections of a shallow baked dish and blank grids for drawing scaled arrangements. In ten pairs, learners represent a doubled quantity in two possible arrangements, mark the surfaces receiving heat, and trace a possible route toward the center. They then explain why doubling quantity alone cannot tell them how long the center takes to reach the supplied safe endpoint. The instructor explicitly states that the drawing is qualitative: heat enters through several surfaces, and distance is not a cooking-time formula.

Allocate 6 minutes to an instructor model, 10 to paired drawings, 8 to explanations and corrections, 6 to writing checking instructions, and 10 to individual transfer. Resources are printed cards, pencils, and an instructor key. No food, devices, preparation, or allergy disclosures are involved.

The unseen individual scenario scales a recipe into thicker portions. Each learner identifies the changed heating distance, rejects an exact time inferred from quantity, and describes a future cook checking the supplied recipe-specific safe endpoint at the specified interior locations, continuing and rechecking if necessary.

Prerequisites are readable diagrams and instructor guidance that prevents treating the picture as a quantitative model. The mechanism could help by connecting a visible geometric change to an otherwise invisible heating process. Its limits include differences in equipment, material, and starting temperature; the classroom task establishes explanatory planning, not practical competence.
SAVE.experiment: Before instruction, give ten learners the drawing task and ten an equally long ingredient-calculation exercise, followed by the same brief individual prompt. Then provide the full model lesson to everyone. Inspect whether drawings produce more explanations connecting changed thickness to uncertain interior heating and an adequate endpoint check. A small falsifying result would be equally frequent fixed-time rules in both groups, or drawing learners claiming that doubled distance means doubled time. Use the final unseen scenario to check all 20 learners individually. This small classroom comparison is diagnostic, not evidence of reliable effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Repair a convincing but unsafe worked solution
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair an attractive reasoning error: correct ingredient arithmetic followed by an unsupported cooking-time calculation. Explicitly separating a valid step from an invalid inference may help adults resist the apparent authority of a neatly worked numerical answer. The central activity is explaining why a plausible solution fails, rather than comparing recipes or rehearsing observation branches.

Prepare printed fictional recipe cards and an accompanying fictional learner solution. For example, the solution correctly triples each ingredient, then triples the cooking time despite placing the mixture in a deeper vessel. Label this as a deliberately flawed teaching example. Supply the original cooking conditions and a recipe-specific safe endpoint. Include another solution that retains the original time with unjustified certainty, so learners do not replace ‘multiply time’ with ‘never change time.’

For 20 adults, spend 5 minutes introducing the task, 7 individually annotating the first solution, 8 discussing repairs in ten pairs, 7 reviewing the second error, 3 writing a replacement instruction, and 10 on individual transfer. All work uses printed materials and pencils; there is no cooking, device use, or request for dietary information.

The transfer card presents a new scaled recipe without a worked answer. Each learner must identify a changed cooking assumption, explain why quantity arithmetic cannot establish the finishing time, and specify a safe future observation against the supplied endpoint, including continuing and rechecking if it is unmet. A time estimate alone does not pass.

What changes the outcome is learning to locate the unsupported inference while preserving the correct arithmetic. Prerequisites include accessible calculations and a clear correction immediately after discussion. Limits include possible reinforcement of the misleading example and learners becoming indiscriminately suspicious of all timing guidance; explicitly retain original times as conditional planning information.
SAVE.experiment: Before the discussion, randomly give half the class the flawed worked solution and half a correct explanation of equal length. Ask both groups to explain the decision on a short new prompt, then teach everyone the complete correction. Compare identification of the unsupported time inference and inclusion of a safe endpoint check. The mechanism is weakened if error diagnosis produces more fixed-time claims, or learners can criticize the supplied answer but cannot generate a safe plan without it. Score the final independent scenario for transfer; do not infer actual cooking safety or durable learning from this single session.
